opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reason is that over the past several years, the dominant recipe has been very simple: take a fairly generic architecture, mostly the Transformer, and scale it up with more data and more compute. That recipe worked remarkably well, so for a while it almost felt like architecture didn't matter. You just pick something reasonable and throw resources at it.

But I think we're starting to see the limits of that approach. High-quality data on the internet is finite, compute is expensive, and the returns from pure scaling are getting smaller. When you can't just keep pushing the scaling knob, the question becomes: how do we get more out of the same data and the same compute? And that's fundamentally a design question. It's about inductive biases, about putting the right structure into the model so it learns more efficiently and generalizes better.

Another reason comes from my own interest in AI for science. In science, we don't just want a model that predicts well. We want to understand what it learned. We want something interpretable, something that can give us symbolic formulas or reveal the underlying structure of a physical system. A giant black-box model isn't naturally good at that. That was part of the motivation behind our work on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: instead of fixed activations on nodes, you put learnable functions on edges, and that makes the model more interpretable and sometimes more parameter-efficient for scientific tasks. Whether or not KANs specifically are the answer, I think the broader point is that different problems may deserve different architectures.

So my view is that the field might move from "one model to rule them all" toward a more diverse ecosystem, where we think carefully about what structure a problem has and design models that respect it. In a way it's going back to how physicists think: you find the right representation first, and then the problem becomes much easier. I think in the post-LLM era, that kind of thinking, which is really about model design, will become much more valuable again.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that for the last few years, model design has been almost boring. The recipe was fixed: take a transformer, make it bigger, feed it more data, and you get a predictable improvement. If scaling alone gives you a reliable curve, nobody has much incentive to question the architecture. Why would you? The gradient is pointing in one direction and everyone just follows it.

But I think we're approaching the point where that gradient flattens. Data is the first wall. We've essentially consumed the high-quality text on the internet, and synthetic data helps but it's not free lunch, because the model is learning from a distribution it generated itself. Compute is the second wall, not because we can't build more chips, but because the returns per dollar are shrinking. When scaling stops being a reliable lever, you're forced to ask the question that was postponed for years: is this actually the right architecture for what we want?

And I'd argue it isn't, for a lot of things. Transformers are remarkable at interpolating within the distribution of human language. But if you look at scientific discovery, or at symbolic reasoning, or at anything that requires the model to find a very compact underlying rule rather than a very large lookup table, the architecture is fighting you. You end up with a model that has memorized ten thousand examples of a pattern instead of learning the one line of math that generates all of them. Those are different kinds of knowledge, and I don't think the current inductive biases favor the second one.

That's really why I spent time on things like KANs, the Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. The point wasn't that it beats transformers at language. It doesn't. The point was to show that if you change the primitive, you change what the network finds easy and what it finds hard, and you change how interpretable the result is. A physicist looking at a KAN can sometimes read off a formula. Nobody reads off a formula from a hundred-billion-parameter attention stack.

So when I say model design becomes more important in the post-LLM era, I mean two things. One is practical: when the scaling curve stops carrying you, architectural choices become the main remaining degree of freedom. The other is more philosophical. We've been treating intelligence as one monolithic thing you can get by piling up parameters. I think the post-LLM era is when we admit that there are different kinds of intelligence, with different structural requirements, and that designing a model is really a statement about what kind of knowledge you want it to represent. That's a design problem, not a scaling problem. And I find that much more exciting than the last five years, frankly.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that, once powerful language models become widely available, the question shifts from “How do we make a bigger model?” to “What kind of model does this particular problem need?”

Language is a very general interface, but it isn’t necessarily the best representation for everything. If you want to understand a physical system, for example, you may care about its dynamics, its symmetries, or conservation laws. A model that incorporates those structures could learn more efficiently and generalize better than one that has to discover everything from data.

So model design is really about deciding what the model should learn and what we should build into it. Scaling has given us a very powerful tool, but it doesn’t eliminate that decision. It can actually make the decision more valuable: we can use language models to help explore architectures, implement ideas, and run experiments, while putting more attention into choosing the right structure.

That’s why I see the post-LLM era as an opportunity for more diversity in models. We’ll still use general-purpose models, but we’ll also want models that are suited to particular scientific questions, computational constraints, and kinds of reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the success of LLMs has shown us how far we can go with a relatively general architecture and a lot of data and compute. But it doesn’t mean architecture no longer matters. It means that, in a regime where scaling works very well, we can afford to pay less attention to some aspects of model design.

As we move toward problems where data is scarce, computation is expensive, or reliability is essential, that tradeoff changes. In science, for example, we often know something about the system already—its symmetries, conservation laws, or underlying structure. The question is how to put that knowledge into a model so it can learn more efficiently and generalize better.

So by the post-LLM era, I don’t necessarily mean an era without LLMs. I mean an era where scaling a language model is no longer the complete answer to every problem. We’ll care more about choosing the right representation, the right inductive biases, and the right computational structure for the task. That makes model design a central research question again.
